claims.text: An intermediate thermal dwell enables sufficient atomic diffusion to overcome local kinetic barriers.
The intermediate dwell suppresses elemental segregation.
The intermediate dwell stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
Rapid heating followed by immediate quenching typically produces phase separation, elemental segregation, and irregular particle morphologies.
A dwell at approximately 500–700 °C can promote homogenization without excessive grain coarsening.
Enhanced atomic diffusion reduces local composition fluctuations and improves homogenization.
Local diffusion during the dwell overcomes short-range ordering and kinetic barriers that cause phase separation.
Balancing mixing enthalpy with configurational entropy during the dwell stabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Precise control of the dwell time–temperature profile prevents excessive particle growth or coarsening.
Dwell-treated nanoparticles will have a more uniform elemental distribution than immediately quenched nanoparticles.
Dwell-treated nanoparticles will exhibit a well-defined single-phase crystal structure, such as FCC.
The intermediate dwell will lower the nanoparticles' thermal decomposition temperature relative to immediate quenching.
A dwell that is too short or too cool will not permit sufficient atomic diffusion.
A dwell that is too long or too hot may cause grain coarsening or secondary-phase formation.
The optimal dwell temperature and duration are material-system dependent.

Failure of the dwell to produce statistically significant improvements in elemental uniformity, phase purity, or decomposition temperature relative to an otherwise identical no-dwell control would falsify the hypothesis.
